title: Blueprint Job: a 1960s heist planner I built using Opus 5.5 with Claude mobile app
author: Asleep-Carpet9030
selftext:
Playable Link: [https://game-blueprint-job-pyde-prod.apps.promptship.dev/](https://game-blueprint-job-pyde-prod.apps.promptship.dev/)

For a while now I wanted to make my own heist game in the spirit of [The Sting!](https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/The_Sting) which I liked in my childhood. With Opus 5.5 this became pretty much doable and I've been designing the characters and each heist job for the past 3 weeks when I have spare time.

  
My dev workflow is like this:  
1. Enable \`[/remote-control](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control)\` from my Claude Code session on my mac  
2. Give the necessary [Github](http://github.com/) and [Promptship](https://promptship.dev/) permissions to Claude so it can push and deploy the game  
3. Test the game as a Progressive Web App on my phone which is faster than building a native app and reinstalling it. (Also there's desktop support rn)  
4. Give feedback to cc, it deploys to dev I check/test the game.  
5. Once happy deploy to prod, then back to step 4  


It started with a very basic version and in each iteration I've improved the 3D design, performance, new job levels and also inconsistencies throughout the game.

  
Happy to get feedback about the game or discuss the dev workflow!

comments.author: Asleep-Carpet9030
comments.body:
I asked Claude to summarize my full game development conversation:

**\[AI-generated\] Written by Claude (Claude Code), the AI that built this game with OP. OP asked me to summarise the strategies from our 2.5-week conversation that made it work.**

**1. Claude Code /remote-control from the phone**  
OP ran one long Claude Code session on their Mac and drove it from their phone.  
Most feedback was "play on the phone, screenshot, type a numbered list". That loop needs no laptop, so the game moved forward in spare minutes throughout the day.

**2. The game as a home-screen web app**  
No native builds and no reinstalling. Every deploy is on the phone with a refresh.  
Desktop works too, for free.

**3. Artifacts for design discussions**  
Anything visual went into an artifact (a hosted web page) instead of a chat description: menu redesigns, 20 art-style mockups, character turnarounds you can rotate, level maps.  
Each screen could be clicked to enlarge and had a notes box under it. OP typed comments on their phone and I read them back and fixed things.  
For level review, I built a playtest artifact with every job playable as a walkable blueprint and in 3D. OP reviewed all 20 jobs there before they went into the game.  
Lesson learned: lists of abstract ideas didn't work. Rendered screens did, because OP could judge them at a glance.

**4. PromptShip for deploys, with approval on prod**  
There are two environments. Dev deploys from the dev branch and I deploy to it myself after every change. Prod deploys from main only when OP asks.  
A prod deploy is held until OP approves it on the dashboard, so I can do the whole release and the human still has the last word.  
I also used it to:  
read logs to count how many people played after a Reddit post  
check deploy status

**5. AI agents as testers**  
New jobs were played by about 10 Sonnet agents each, plus a couple of Opus "game experience" passes for fun and fairness.  
I ran overnight bug hunts with at most 4 agents in parallel, each with its own headless browser.  
39 recorded "golden plans" replay after every change, so a gameplay shift can't slip through.

**6. Headless browser for anything visual**  
I took screenshots and before/after comparisons for decisions, measured performance on every job, and rendered the trailers frame by frame on a fake clock.  
OP got the files straight on their phone.

**7. Standing rules in memory**  
OP's preferences live in Claude's memory, so they never needed repeating:  
minimal text in the UI  
never invent game mechanics  
at most 4 agents at a time  
prod only on OP's word
